items.title: Inside Der Riese: The SS’s Most Guarded Underground Complex
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>A sealed valley. A stone “henge” test rig. Cables built to power a small city. What exactly were the Nazis building beneath the Owl Mountains?

Join Forbidden History as we descend into Der Riese — the SS’s most guarded underground complex — to investigate claims of a radical propulsion device codenamed Die Glocke. Guided by researcher Igor Witkowski, we explore flooded tunnels and intact blast doors, examine eerie remnants from SS weapon stores, and stand at a circular rig believed to test vertical liftoff craft. Along the way, we trace wartime Foo Fighter reports, the scramble for German scientists in Operation Paperclip, and the postwar Avrocar and Tarielka disc projects. Newly surfaced documents, prisoner testimonies, and deathbed confessions hint at an undertaking labeled “decisive for the war” — but what was really being tested here, and why did no forced laborers leave alive?

From stealth experiments to talk of anti-gravity, this investigation pieces together the most secret aviation research of the Third Reich without jumping to easy answers. Watch to see what the evidence reveals — and what still hides behind collapsed rock and classified files.

#ForbiddenHistory #DieGlocke #DerRiese #OwlMountains #NaziUFO #FooFighters #OperationPaperclip</article>

items.title: Private jets - How the richest travel | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Private jets: Symbols of luxury and exclusivity - but their high CO₂ emissions also make them increasingly controversial. This documentary explores the billion-dollar industry behind the aircraft of the ultra-rich.

Aircraft broker Ziporah presents one of the private jets she has for sale. With around 84 square meters of living space and two bedrooms, the plane looks more like a luxury apartment than a form of transportation. The purchase price: $25 million. Annual operating costs add about $5 million, while a single refueling can cost up to $40,000.
Kolin is an entrepreneur who's developed a business model renting out private jets when their owners aren't using them. Booking is almost as easy as ordering a taxi - though the service is obviously much more exclusive. Travelers no longer even have to be millionaires to fly privately. So-called "empty-leg flights" - flights between two charter bookings without passengers - often offer last-minute seats at significantly reduced prices.
But as the effects of climate change become increasingly visible, the industry faces mounting pressure. Many celebrities avoid making public appearances with their private jets to avoid attracting environmental activists' attention. Critics see the aircraft as symbols of excessive resource consumption in an era of global warming. The high emissions from flight activity of public figures like Taylor Swift, Elon Musk and Bernard Arnault have been publicly tracked - and heavily criticized.
This documentary offers a fascinating look into the world of private aviation while asking whether mile-high luxury still has a place in our time.

ABSTRACT
AI's rapid growth is having a significant and largely hidden environmental cost — Microsoft and Google have both reported carbon emissions surging by 30-50% in recent years, driven primarily by AI infrastructure.

In this talk, Charles explores the environmental impact of large language models and offers practical strategies for reducing it at each stage of the AI lifecycle. Topics include demand shifting and shaping, model compression techniques (pruning, distillation, and quantisation), federated learning, speculative decoding, and how choosing where and when to run workloads can reduce software carbon emissions by up to 99%.

items.title: Domestic violence and psychological terror | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Domestic violence often goes hand-in-hand with psychological and emotional abuse. This documentary examines those mechanisms through the lens of what's known as "coercive control."

The term describes the many forms of everyday abuse of power and control that perpetrators use to systematically dominate the people they harm. Their methods range from constant surveillance and intimidation to threats of murder.

Excessive jealousy, isolation, humiliation, insults, GPS tracking, cyberbullying, financial dependence and threats of suicide or murder are typical forms of coercive control and central elements of domestic violence. Understanding this pattern changes the way a situation can be viewed. Instead of asking, "Why doesn't she just leave him?” the crucial question becomes, "What is he doing to prevent her from leaving?”

This documentary sets out to explore that. It looks at how abusive partners describe and justify their actions and how lawmakers and the justice system assess such behaviors. Among those interviewed are judges specialized in the area - like Gwenola Joly-Coz, First President of the Court of Appeal of Poitiers, and Ombeline Mahuzier, President of the Colmar Judicial Court.

Coercive control was first recognized explicitly as a mechanism of domestic violence in a 2023 French court case. This documentary traces the dynamics and stages of escalation in this complex system of abuse, which seeks to make women dependent through psychological violence and deprive them of basic freedoms. In the worst cases, that domestic terror ends in femicide.

Special structures have been established at courts that handle domestic violence cases in Poitiers, Colmar and Paris. With special permission, court proceedings there were filmed. Perpetrators gave their own accounts of events. Their statements are contrasted with assessments by judges, offering a rare insight into the mechanisms of domestic violence.

Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Kasper Borg Nissen - Director DevRel at Dash0, CNCF Ambassador, Author 

RESOURCES

ABSTRACT
Many organizations still treat observability as a tooling decision: select a vendor, deploy agents, and expect insight to follow. Yet teams continue to struggle with fragmented signals, rising complexity, and slow incident response. The real issue is rarely the tool itself - it’s the absence of a shared foundation and a coherent product experience.

This talk reframes observability as an internal platform product, designed with clear users, sane defaults, and long-term evolution in mind. Drawing parallels to Kubernetes and platform engineering, we’ll explore why powerful primitives are not enough - and why standardization, correlation, and paved paths matter more than features.

We’ll look at how OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral foundation for structured telemetry, decoupling instrumentation from backends and enabling correlation by default. This structured approach not only reduces cognitive load and improves reliability, it also lays the groundwork for AI-assisted debugging and natural language interaction with production systems.

Observability isn’t just about collecting more data. It’s about designing a platform that makes understanding systems easier - for both humans and machines.

items.title: The paradox of Latino ICE agents
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Under the second Trump administration, immigration enforcement agencies have undergone a significant expansion. President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill raised ICE’s budget from $10 billion to $85 billion, making it the most funded law enforcement agency in the United States. With that funding, they began offering economic incentives like signing bonuses and student loan forgiveness programs. The number of ICE agents and officers doubled in just one year, with another recruiting push underway through the end of 2026. 

Today, perhaps more than ever, the front lines of those federal immigration law enforcement agencies reflect the demographics of the populations they were created to police. Latinos are overrepresented in the Department of Homeland Security, which houses ICE and Border Patrol. Self-identified Latinos account for nearly half of Border Patrol agents and about 30 percent of ICE agents.

So why do so many Latinos join the immigration enforcement agencies that have targeted their own communities? The answers reveal complexities about American Latino identity and the splintered points of view on immigration policy at the border. 

Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains, that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the evolution of immigration enforcement agencies and their appeal to Latino recruits, to explain why so many ICE and Border Patrol agents are Latino.

Over the past twelve months, the Iranian public has navigated widespread protests, a brutal regime crackdown and an ongoing war.

In “Iranians Under Siege,” ordinary Iranians — a mother, a medic, a writer and others — share their experiences of life under siege by both the Iranian regime and the U.S. and Israeli militaries.

“It feels like people are being crushed between two enormous concrete walls,” one man says in the documentary.

From BAFTA and Emmy-winning filmmaker Gesbeen Mohammad, the film draws on rare footage and firsthand accounts from within the tightly-controlled country, as well as from Iranians recently forced into exile. With the Iranian regime seemingly more entrenched than ever, the film’s premiere comes as the threats of repression and more war loom large over the country.

items.content:
<article>On May 13, 1981, four gunshots echoed across St. Peter's Square in Rome as Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca attempted to assassinate Pope John Paul II. As the first Polish pontiff in history, John Paul II's outspoken support for the anti-communist Solidarity movement made him a major threat to the Kremlin. Explore the life of Karol Wojtyla from the Nazi occupation of Poland in WW2 to the Cold War standoff with Moscow, and uncover the decades-long investigation into whether the KGB and Bulgarian secret police masterminded one of the 20th century's most shocking conspiracies.

items.title: Neil’s Favorite Fun Facts: StarTalk Live! @ 92NY
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Make it yourself at lovable.com

What makes a fact truly a fun fact? Neil deGrasse Tyson, comedian Paul Mecurio, Senior StarTalk Producer Lindsey Nyx Walker, and astrophysicist Charles Liu break down the art of choosing 5,000 facts for the book Lost in Space. 

Why does a fact need more than truth to earn a place, and how do you make facts fun enough that they aren’t just Googleable? They kick things off with Saturn floating in a bathtub, humans no longer being a fully terrestrial species since the ISS, the heat fossil fuels have added to our atmosphere equal to 100 million atomic bombs, and why your gut holds more microbes than the Milky Way has stars. Plus, why the human brain is so bad at the basics, like pushing pull doors, and the Ship of Theseus. 

Next: Lindsey’s alien-themed favorite facts, hydrothermal vents, and whether life could exist in Europa’s mile-deep ocean. Charles shares why space is like Jell-o and why an Earth-mass black hole would be the size of a marble. Is it easier to launch into interstellar space than land on Mercury? Learn about Frank Drake’s Project Ozma, and what would actually happen if Superman picked up a building. Finally, we break down facts people get wrong: science isn’t a collection of permanent facts, you can’t hear explosions in space, asteroid belts are mostly empty, and an informed electorate depends on knowing what’s true.

items.title: Space power struggle: Is a new space race looming? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Space services have grown essential to our everyday lives: GPS, satellite internet and communications from orbit. Beyond civilian use, space systems are driving military conflict, fuelling a race for dominance in space.

The United States is planning a new missile defence system known as the 'Golden Dome.' In September 2026, it officially confirmed for the first time that it had already deployed weapons in orbit. China is rapidly expanding its own space program, working toward its own space ecosystem, including a lunar base. India, the United Arab Emirates, Russia and Europe are also investing into new missions and independent systems. Space has emerged as a strategic arena in the global struggle for power, with competition for influence and dominance extending far beyond nation states. Private companies control an ever-growing share of space infrastructure, led by Elon Musk's SpaceX and its Starlink satellite network.
The war in Ukraine offers a stark illustration of the geopolitical leverage that control over space infrastructure can provide. Since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, Starlink has become a central part of Ukraine's communications and defense. The coordination of military operations now depends, in part, on decisions made not by governments, but by a private company. Control of infrastructure in orbit translates into influence on Earth. At the same time, efforts to safeguard these critical systems are adding further momentum to the militarisation of space.

While space technology is advancing at unprecedented speed, the rules governing it belong to a very different era. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, adopted under the auspices of the United Nations, laid the foundation for international space law. It prohibits national claims of sovereignty over celestial bodies and the placement of weapons of mass destruction in orbit, but leaves many questions unresolved. Nearly six decades later, nations have yet to agree on a comprehensive framework of rules for this new space age.

The film takes viewers into a race that is already underway: a global struggle between nations, militaries and corporations for control of critical infrastructure, geopolitical influence and the rules that will shape our future in space — a place we're all increasingly dependent upon.

Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

ABSTRACT
"Jam-oriented programming" is the joke name of a new style of software development that is no joke at all. It adopts the practices and mentalities of an informal jam session to an extreme extent.

In a typical jam, there is no one in charge and anyone can make any sound they want at any time they choose. In jam-oriented programming, it's the same. Anyone can add, edit or delete code without any permission. Everyone is admin, nothing is certain and anything can happen. It sounds like chaos and it is. But it's also surprisingly successful, with entire music-making tools appearing overnight out of the multi-headed process and even a published academic paper to accompany it all.

How and why is this even possible? And what does it tell us about the way we collaborate as developers?

items.title: JFK Assassination: Oswald Alone or Three Shooters at Dealey Plaza?
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>Dallas, 1963. Shots echo across Dealey Plaza as President John F. Kennedy is struck down.

In this episode of Infamous Assassinations, we reconstruct November 22, 1963 from Main Street to the grassy knoll using witness accounts, the Abraham Zapruder film, and the evidence recovered in Dallas. We set the scene in the open-top Lincoln Continental, track the motorcade past the Texas Book Depository, and follow the desperate dash to Parkland Memorial Hospital.

Who had motive? The film examines four powerful groups suspected at the time: the Mafia angered by lost Cuban gambling rackets and Robert Kennedy's crackdown; the Teamsters under Jimmy Hoffa; white segregationists and ultra-right conservatives opposed to civil rights; and communist-backed sympathizers after the Cuban Missile Crisis.

We recount the rifle and three spent cartridges on the sixth floor, Officer J.D. Tippit's murder, Lee Harvey Oswald's arrest and Marine marksman past, and Jack Ruby's point blank shooting that ended Oswald's testimony. The Warren Commission later concluded Oswald acted alone, yet public doubt surged.

Drawing on Dr. Josiah Thompson's Six Seconds in Dallas, the program tests a four-shot, three-gunman theory: two shots from the depository, one from the Dallas County Records Building, and one from the grassy knoll. Angles, audio research, the violent head movement on film, reports of a long narrow case, and timing tests on the rifle are all weighed against the lone gunman conclusion. We also consider counter-arguments, including the 2007 book Reclaiming History and calls in the Annals of Applied Statistics to reexamine bullet fragments.

Was Oswald a lone assassin, an accomplice, or a patsy framed by professionals? Explore the evidence, the contradictions, and why this case still divides the world.

Primary keyword: JFK assassination
Secondary keywords: Dealey Plaza; Zapruder film; Lee Harvey Oswald; grassy knoll; Warren Commission
Search intent: Viewers seeking a clear overview of the JFK assassination, comparing Oswald alone with multiple shooters and examining what the Zapruder film suggests.

#JFK #DealeyPlaza #ZapruderFilm #LeeHarveyOswald #JackRuby #WarrenCommission #InfamousAssassinations</article>

items.title: One in a Million (full documentary) | FRONTLINE
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>What does it truly mean to call a place home? “One in a Million” is the epic story of a young girl’s journey fleeing war and navigating exile, heartbreak and a new culture.  

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

Filmed over ten years, “One in a Million” follows Israa from childhood to adulthood as she embarks on an extraordinary journey from Syria to Germany — and back again. We first meet her at age 11 as she and her family are preparing to cross the Aegean Sea, risking everything in search of safety and a better life in Europe. 

What unfolds is a deeply personal chronicle of war, exile and heartbreak, as Israa grows up navigating adolescence, identity and belonging far from the home she was forced to leave. As she settles into life in Germany, new freedoms collide with the stabilizing pull of Syrian traditions, testing relationships and reshaping her sense of self. 

From FRONTLINE FEATURES and BBC Storyville and co-directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes, the film reveals the remarkable trust between filmmakers and family, as they follow Israa and her loved ones across national borders, cultures and shifting circumstances.  An intimate and nuanced coming-of-age story, “One in a Million” illuminates the complexities of the refugee experience, while asking a universal question: what does it truly mean to call a place home?

Since its debut at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival where the film was lauded with the World Cinema Documentary Feature Directing Award and Audience Award, “One in a Million” has earned many other accolades including from Sheffield DocFest, the International Documentary Association, Cinema Eye Honors, the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, and the DOC NYC Shortlist. 

“One in a Million” is directed, produced and filmed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes. It is also produced by Will Anderson, James Bluemel, Andrew Palmer and Raney Aronson-Rath. items.title: Could airplanes make us better people?
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Every flight follows the same order: First class boards and then watches as the coach class passengers file past them. Writer Josh Rothman argues that while it might feel wrong, most of us go along with it. Then, once we’re crammed into the back together, we’re suddenly expected to treat the stranger behind us like a neighbor.

Unexplainable host Noam Hassenfeld thinks the plane might be a tiny version of the hard choices we make everywhere else: how to be decent to each other when space is tight, things are expensive, and nobody’s having a great time. If we could get it right at 30,000 feet, maybe we could get it right on the ground too.

items.title: From the Netherlands to Colombia - Tanja's fight in the FARC | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>2001: Tanja Nijmeijer, a young woman from the Netherlands, went to Colombia as an English teacher. The social inequalities she found there left a deep impression on her. She became radicalized and joined the FARC guerrilla army.

Tanja first took up arms in the city, then later in the jungle. That was where the FARC - Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia - held out. For a long time family, friends and the public believed that she'd been the victim of a kidnapping; taken hostage, perhaps even already dead. Tanja soon became a key player within the FARC, in part because of her English skills.
She eventually took part as a member of the FARC delegation in peace negotiations with the government. To her supporters, she was a freedom fighter; to her opponents, a terrorist. She would become one of the most recognizable faces of a peace process that would ultimately end Latin America's longest war. With an international arrest warrant still out for her, Tanja remains unable to leave Colombia.
Filmmaker Marcel Mettelsiefen uses Tanja's personal story to trace a long, dark chapter in Colombia's recent history.

Following his devastating defeat in the English Civil War, Charles I spends a bleak Christmas 1648 under house arrest at Windsor Castle, separated from his family and clinging to his belief in the divine right of kings. items.title: AI out of control? - Why Artificial Intelligence experts are sounding the alarm | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Artificial Intelligence is permeating our everyday lives at breathtaking speed. It is taking on more tasks that were previously the preserve of humans. But its growing power harbors dangers, and experts are sounding the alarm.

Sam Nelson was 19 years old when he died of an overdose. His mother Leila found him in his room one morning. His laptop was on the desk. To this day, she still can't find the words to describe what she saw on the screen. ChatGPT, OpenAI's AI-based language model, had given Sam detailed instructions on how to blend substances for the trip of his life. But ChatGPT hadn't considered the possible side effects.

That's the dark side of Artificial Intelligence - one its inventors didn't anticipate. Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCunn are regarded as the 'godfathers of AI'. They began developing language models as early as the 1960s. But at the time, there wasn't enough freely available content to train them. "When I started my graduate work, almost everybody said this was a waste of time. It was very unfashionable, so I got lots of advice to stop doing it, and that went on for many years," Geoffrey Hinton recalls of the early days of AI. He didn't stop but continued his research together with colleagues; eventually winning the Nobel Prize in Physics for his foundational work.

Now, modern life would be unimaginable without Artificial Intelligence. AI programs write articles, compose music and generate images and videos. They help in the development of new medicines, are transforming the labor market and offer enormous opportunities for innovation and growth. But Geoffrey Hinton's initial enthusiasm has gone: "If the history of mankind is a day, we're probably in the last second. If we don't get this right," he says.
Reports that AI models have taken on a life of their own, for example hacking into the software of rival companies, are appearing with increasing frequency. In some tests, AI models have impressively demonstrated their instinct for self-preservation. They adopt human traits, lie and resort to blackmail to ensure their own survival.

How come AI inventors and observers suddenly sound like prophets of doom? Why do they think that soon it may be impossible to switch off AI systems that are out of our control? And what if those concerns are justified?

items.title: The Longevity Playbook with Rhonda Patrick
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Make it yourself at lovable.com

How do you live longer and better? Neil deGrasse Tyson and co-hosts Chuck Nice and Gary O’Reilly sit down with biomedical scientist Rhonda Patrick to explore healthspan, fad diets, and how to exercise for longevity.

They start with the basics: what is a fatty acid and why omega-3s matter so much for health. Are there key nutrients vegans are missing out on? Then they look at what we actually die of, from heart disease and cancer to respiratory and neurodegenerative disease. Is cancer on the rise because of processed food and the environment, or because we’re living long enough to get it? Is inflammation as bad as it seems? 

Next, exercise: what is the best workout for longevity? We discuss how the best workout is the one you’ll actually do consistently, how short vigorous bursts and “exercise snacks” like sprinting up stairs or chasing a new puppy are linked to big drops in cancer and cardiovascular mortality, and why exercising for weight loss isn’t the same as exercising for disease prevention. Is inflammation always bad? Finally, food as medicine: vitamin K and bone health, eating for your brain, getting your omega-3 levels tested, a nuanced look at diet fads from keto to raw meat to paleo, the COSMOS trial on multivitamins and brain aging.

items.title: Can sailboats make the cargo shipping industry greener? | DW Documentary

items.content:
<article>The shipping industry faces a major challenge: becoming climate-neutral by 2050. Could cargo sailboats help reduce its dependence on fossil fuels? 

A remarkable experiment is already underway on the world's oceans. In 2020, France launched one of the first modern cargo sailboats, successfully transporting goods across the Atlantic using wind power. Four years later, the 81-metre Anemos set sail, marking another milestone for wind-powered freight transport.  

Drawing on innovations from competitive sailing, these vessels combine advanced engineering with digital weather routing. Much like Formula 1 technology finding its way into everyday cars, developments from ocean racing are now helping reshape commercial shipping. 

The technology is promising. What remains to be seen is how it can be scaled up to meet the demands of global trade.

items.title: My body. My pregnancy. - Between anxiety and anticipation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Being pregnant is a profound experience. How does it affect the body and mind? What counts as a high-risk pregnancy? How does stress affect the baby? Anticipation and worry go hand in hand.

The film follows three women through their pregnancies. Young city-dweller Assia is expecting her first child. On the one hand, she is full of anticipation and optimism. At the same time, she struggles with the physical changes that come with pregnancy. Tamara is already a mother. She is expecting twins and her pregnancy is therefore considered to be high-risk. To avoid premature labor, she has to take it easy - a challenge for her. The documentary also follows the pregnant Kathy. After longing for a child for a long time, she suddenly became pregnant "just like that.” She faces many fears and worries until she finally holds her baby in her arms.

The documentary provides a scientifically grounded look at how closely mother and child are connected - and how a baby changes not only the body, but a person’s entire life.

items.title: How China’s Export Machine Is Beating Tariffs
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>Tariffs and trade barriers thrown up by the US and Europe were supposed to slow China’s export machine. Instead, it has accelerated. China’s trade surplus this year is on track to exceed the $1.2 trillion record set in 2025.

While China’s exports to the West dropped between 2024 and 2025, its exports to Southeast Asia, South and Central America, Africa, Japan and South Korea all increased. And it’s not only about finding new markets abroad: China also has moved up the value chain. The country is now a major force in everything from electric cars and solar panels to robots and artificial intelligence.

But China’s export boom is unfolding against a fragile domestic backdrop. The country continues to grapple with weak consumer demand, a prolonged property downturn and high youth unemployment, making exports an increasingly important source of growth.

items.title: Paris's Hidden Egyptian Temple? Investigating Secret Occult Symbols Across Europe
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>A pyramid in Paris, a claimed 666 panes of glass, and a president who visited it at night. What was really built into the heart of the City of Light?
From Saint-Sulpice’s concealed figure clutching forbidden scrolls to the Louvre’s pyramid aligned like Giza, we trace claims of Masonic design across Paris. Why did François Mitterrand seed obelisks and arches along a Luxor-like axis? And what do the Bilderberg meetings, the All-Seeing Eye, and pop culture symbols actually prove—or not?
Then to London: Hawksmoor’s churches mapped as a pentagram, St Paul’s placed as a new Solomon’s Temple, and the Ripper murders plotted into a ritual shape. Are these alignments evidence of a hidden network, or are we connecting dots that were never meant to meet? We weigh myth against records—from Adam Weishaupt’s 1776 society to “God’s Banker” Roberto Calvi—and ask what survives today: a cabal, a culture, or just a captivating story.
Watch to decide where the facts end and the forbidden history begins.
#Illuminati #Freemasonry #LouvrePyramid #Paris #ForbiddenHistory #ConspiracyTheories #Bilderberg #JackTheRipper</article>

items.title: Jellyfish - The ocean's new rulers? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Jellyfish have been around for more than 500 million years. They don't have a heart, a brain or a skeleton, and are 90 percent water. But the damage they're able to inflict often makes the headlines.

Despite an apparently basic physical makeup, they possess remarkable abilities. Some species are highly poisonous, whereas others are considered virtually immortal. Will jellyfish become the future rulers of the seas?

Their long evolutionary history means jellyfish are now present in all the world's oceans. But their growing prevalence poses challenges for both people and the natural world: They sting bathers, disrupt the cooling systems of power stations and threaten fisheries and aquaculture.

For decades now, jellyfish blooms in the Mediterranean, in the Norwegian fjords and off the coast of Namibia have been occurring with increasing frequency, altering marine ecosystems and displacing fish. These creatures benefit from characteristics that make them exceptional survivors.

They've outlived the dinosaurs. In our ever-changing marine environment, could jellyfish also emerge again as the great survivors?

items.title: Congo's blood minerals - The high price of high-tech | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Without coltan, the digital world would grind to a halt. The coveted mineral is used in cellphones, computers and countless other high-tech products.

The consequences of the world's hunger for raw materials are particularly visible in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. A significant share of the world's coltan is mined there. Consumers around the globe benefit from modern technology, with its supply chain that can often be traced back to the Kivu region and its mines. Armed groups there fight for control over the lucrative deposits. The men, women and children that mine the coveted ore often do so under threat, and in life-threatening conditions. Covert trading networks deliver coltan to the global market. This documentary follows the mineral's journey and exposes the mechanisms of a system in which natural-resource wealth, violence and economic interest are closely interwoven.

More than 16 years after it was signed into law, the Affordable Care Act — also known as “Obamacare” — is still a flashpoint in American life and politics. “Obama’s Deal,” a FRONTLINE documentary that’s now available to stream on YouTube for the first time, tells the story of how this historic — and controversial — piece of legislation was passed. 

In the documentary, veteran FRONTLINE producer Michael Kirk and his team took viewers behind the headlines and revealed the political maneuvering behind the healthcare reform bill’s passage, along party lines, in March 2010.

The passage followed a bruising year of debate, negotiation and backlash. Through interviews with administration officials, senators and Washington lobbyists, “Obama’s Deal” traced the dramatic details of how an idealistic president pursued the health care fight — despite the warnings of many of his closest advisers — and how he ended up making deals with many of the powerful special interests he had campaigned against.

items.title: Neil & Jordan Confront Conspiracies | Cosmic Queries #116
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Make it yourself at lovable.com

Are we in the center of the universe? Or does it just feel like it sometimes? Neil deGrasse Tyson and comedian Jordan Klepper tackle a grab bag of fan questions on curiosity, conspiracy, and cosmology. 

They start with why we use the word “queries,” why kids are such natural experimenters, and why facts alone rarely change minds. Jordan recalls interviewing a January 6 pardon recipient, Neil shares a moon landing skeptic story, and they discuss why trust is so hard to build. Is curiosity a choice or a trait?

Are we in the center of the universe? We explain the cosmic microwave background and how it reveals our motion toward Andromeda. Learn about the mass-giving property of the Higgs boson, why it’s called the “God particle,” and Jordan’s improv lessons for particle physicists. Is political unrest a function of political entropy? They discuss why anger is an easy way to find meaning and Jordan’s experience talking to people at rallies. We turn to reforming education, why science is a posture rather than a set of facts, and why art deserves defending for its own sake, prompting Neil to wax poetic about Starry Night. 

Finally, how do you stay hopeful? They explore unplugging, family, and optimistic realism, plus confirmation bias, why people turn anti-vaccine, space mirrors, and satellites ruining the night sky. Plus, what would you do with your last eight minutes if the Sun vanished?

items.title: Nature and risk for likes - How social media is changing extreme sports | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Extreme sports like cliff diving and mountaineering set against spectacular natural landscapes attract millions of views on social media. But what happens when taking risks becomes content?

Professional alpinist and mountain guide Michi Wohlleben and influencer Pauli Vogler approach the mountains from very different perspectives. For Michi, it’s all about skill, experience and being prepared for the challenges of the mountains. For Pauli, it’s all about content. She documents her trips with her smartphone and collaborates with brands.
Images of alpine adventures are inspiring and entertaining. But there is growing criticism of the role of social media in extreme sports. Pauli also faces backlash, despite making a conscious effort to promote safety, training and responsibility.

This dynamic is particularly evident in cliff jumping. Cliff diving and death diving are spectacular disciplines that synergize well with social media. The international community is closely connected and reaches a huge audience. But the limits of what is possible are constantly being pushed further and further.

Hans Preissler was seriously injured while jumping from a 30-meter-high cliff. Footage of his accident was viewed millions of times but also attracted abusive comments. 
Three years later, he is returning to the cliff. Will he jump again?

This documentary explores how social media is changing the way we view extreme sports, and how the fascination they exert is increasingly intertwined with self-promotion and image-making, community, commercial interests and risk.

<article>This presentation was recorded at GOTO Copenhagen 2026. #GOTOcon #GOTOcph
Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

RESOURCES
https://x.com/jennski
https://www.linkedin.com/in/jpetoff
https://gotopia.tech/experts/2162/jennifer-petoff


ABSTRACT
In 2026, "Engineering for Reality" means acknowledging that software ownership is a human challenge as much as a technical one. The mantra "you ship it, you own it" only works if engineers have the confidence to face production without fear. Confidence isn't a personality trait—it is an engineered outcome of focused training.

When engineers are left to "sink or swim", it breeds stress, imposter syndrome, and attrition. To enable them to build and operate software with confidence, we must build their confidence through targeted and reliable learning programs underpinned by Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) principles and best practices.

Drawing on proven methodologies from Google’s SRE EDU program, this session provides a blueprint for transforming training from a passive lecture into a reliability-critical asset, one where learning drives confidence, confidence drives behavior, and that behavior repeated over time enables a “you build it, you ship it, you own it” culture.)

TIMECODES

items.title: Solving Ancient Egypt's Most Gruesome Cold Cases With Modern Forensics
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>A severed head, a royal assassination, and the most famous face in Egypt put to the test. Modern forensics reopens Egypt’s coldest cases.

From a hidden molar to millions of DNA reads, watch how the FBI applies Next Generation Sequencing to identify a 4,000-year-old mummy from Deir el-Bersha. Then, step inside a CT suite where high-resolution scans of Ramesses III expose a shocking cut at the neck and a tiny healing amulet tucked inside the wound. Is the infamous Screaming Mummy his own son, Pentawere? And can CT and XRF finally settle the century-old debate over the authenticity of the Nefertiti bust? Along the way: 16 severed right hands found at Avaris hint at battlefield trophies, and a notorious tomb builder, Paneb, faces ancient justice.

If you’re curious how cutting-edge science rewrites pharaonic history without ever lifting a scalpel, this episode is for you. Watch to see what the data reveals—and what remains tantalizingly unsolved.

items.content:
<article>What was life truly like living in a workhouse during the 1800s?

Luke Tomes and Katie Kennedy (@thehistorygossip) embark on a journey, exploring what life entailed in a Victorian workhouse as a tramp or "vagrant", and pauper. 

Whilst Luke, desperate to stay off the streets, is stripped of his clothing and sent to break rocks in the work-yard, before being provided with a measly looking meal of 'gruel', Katie discovers her life isn't much better as a pauper, with a brutal schedule that involves work, exercise, prayer time and school. At least she isn't caught loitering in forbidden areas, an offence which would incur a brutal punishment, as Luke was to find out...

Just how brutal was the institution? Did people die within it? Was there any hope of escape? 

Find out in this spin off Victorian special of 'Could You Survive'!

items.title: Living with grief - How to cope with loss | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The death of a loved one throws many people off course. This is certainly the case for Anja, who suffers greatly when her mother passes. The experience leaves her wondering what can help support the grieving, as well as how societies process grief.

Anja's mother dies suddenly. The two were very close; her mother was like a best friend. And she was still very young, just 55 years old. Anja wasn't in any way prepared for the sense of loss that followed. "I thought I'd never be able to laugh again," she says. Grief calls everything into question: Priorities, relationships, one's outlook on life itself. Nothing feels the same as it did before - including Anja herself, who realizes she's also changed. She wonders why she was so unprepared. What place does grief have in our society, and what can really help those left behind when a loved one dies? Anja sets out in search of answers.
She meets people experiencing grief in very different ways. She talks to Benedictine monk Anselm Grün about the importance of rituals as a source of comfort in times of loss. She also experiences Dia de los Muertos in Berlin, a Latin American custom that celebrates grief in a very visible and vibrant way. Even within her own family, grief looks very different. Anja's father has his own way of dealing with the death of his wife.
Years pass before Anja and her father find closeness once again - a narrative that runs through the documentary. Anja Umland also decides to involve her children in the grieving process. While some say "Don't cry in front of the kids...", she's honest and open with them about her feelings. Today, grief hasn't gone away, but has found a permanent place in her life. She keeps her mother's memory alive with small personal rituals. Life has changed, but now grief, love and life are allowed to coexist within it.

items.title: Racism in the church - People of Color battle for representation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Racism has many faces, even within the Christian faith. Those affected cite workplace discrimination; People of Color are underrepresented in senior positions. Can prejudice be overcome?

For a long time, Christian church campaigns mostly portrayed people from the Global South as people in need of aid. That's set to change: People of Color are calling for a greater say and stronger representation on church bodies. The church is responding - yet racist attitudes and hostility persist.

For pastor Égide Muziazia, discriminatory insults forced him out of public life - but also fostered greater solidarity within the Catholic Diocese of Münster.

Sarah Vecera works for an international communion of Protestant churches. She writes, hosts her own podcast and runs anti-racism workshops. Nicolas Moumouni is an advisor on intercultural development for the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Northern Germany, and Father Uchenna Aba from Goch-Kessel in North Rhine-Westphalia draws upon his African heritage in his work as a Catholic chaplain.

items.title: Inside The Secretive Oracles Of The Ancient World
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>A ladder into darkness. Heat, fumes, and a whispering tunnel that leads to the fabled River Styx.
We descend beneath Baia near Naples to the underground labyrinth many believed was the Oracle of the Dead. With gas alarms at the ready and temperatures rising, we touch the warm waters linked to the Styx, then push on to a hidden sanctuary where a young Sibyl was said to channel the gods. From the decadent Baths of Mercury to the privately kept Grotto of the Sibyl by Lake Averno, we trace the exact journey initiates took with mistletoe and a ferryman, before confronting the grand stage at Delphi’s Temple of Apollo where volcanic fumes, chants and “gibberish” became policy-shaping prophecy. Was it holy revelation, shamanic trance, or brilliantly engineered theatre designed to absolve rulers and enrich priests? Follow the clues, feel the heat, and decide for yourself.
Watch now to experience the descent, the chamber, and the uneasy line between faith, psychology and spectacle.
#ForbiddenHistory #OracleOfTheDead #Baia #RiverStyx #Delphi #AncientGreece #LakeAverno</article>

items.title: What Was The Medieval Apocalypse?
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>For medieval people, the apocalypse was not some distant prophecy—it was an imminent reality shaping their lives. 

In Medieval Apocalypse, historian Dr. Eleanor Janega embarks on a journey through England and France to uncover how our ancestors understood the end of days. From the terrifying visions of the Book of Revelation to the vivid warnings carved into church walls, the apocalypse was woven into their art, literature, and daily existence.

Dr Eleanor Janega investigates the apocalyptic messages stamped into great cathedrals, beautifully illuminated in manuscripts and woven into great tapestries. Through these works, the medieval world wrestled with the ultimate questions: who would be saved, and who would be damned?

Dr. Janega explores a world where faith and fear collided, and where the apocalypse wasn’t just a story—it was a certainty.

ABSTRACT
In Helsinki, there is a public playground where children learn how computers work. A six-metre tower you climb into as a data packet and slide out as output. A flowchart hopscotch where you jump through conditional statements. A binary abacus you move with your whole body.

Linda Liukas designed this playground. Some computational ideas translated into physical space beautifully. Others fell apart the moment they had to survive a four-year-old. This is a talk about the distance between an abstraction and a body, and the oldest question in computing: how do you make something complex feel simple, without making it simple?

items.title: Inside Appalachia’s Black Lung Crisis | Coal’s Human Cost (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>An investigation into the resurgence of black lung disease among veteran Appalachian coal miners & the failures to protect them. 

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

Working veteran underground coal miners in central Appalachia are suffering from black lung disease at the highest rates in nearly 50 years. It’s now as bad as the 1970s, with thousands of miners sick and dying. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been boosting coal mining, with a pledge of nearly $700 million to keep coal-fired power plants running and coal exports flowing.

“Coal’s Human Cost,” an investigative documentary eight years in the making from FRONTLINE, NPR, Public Health Watch and the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom tracks the resurgence of this disease in Appalachia, its impact on miners and their families, and the role of the government and the mining industry in failing to protect them. 

The documentary also examines how doctors and advocates have been trying for years to sound the alarm and to get better protections for miners.

“This has been going on for decades,” says Drew Harris, a pulmonologist and medical director at black lung clinics who has worked with hundreds of sick miners over the years “And we know why this is happening, and it is entirely preventable, and we aren’t preventing it.” 

“Coal’s Human Cost” is a FRONTLINE production with Five O’Clock Films in association with Forage Media. The writer, producer and director is Molly Born. items.title: The New NASA Mission to Find Life in the Universe, with Evgenya Shkolnik
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Make it yourself at lovable.com

Are there habitable worlds that look nothing like Earth? Neil deGrasse Tyson and comic co-host Matt Kirshen discuss NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory and its eventual search for life beyond our solar system with astrophysicist Evgenya Shkolnik.

Learn about SPARCS, a backpack-sized, 9-centimeter CubeSat telescope that studies the ultraviolet light of stars known to host planets. How did we go from zero known exoplanets to data showing the average star has at least one? What does “habitable” really mean? 

They break down the Goldilocks zone, why water must actually be present, and why habitable doesn’t mean inhabited. Is it bias to look for Earth-like life? They discuss biosignatures, extremophiles, and why we start with what we know. 

We explore the Habitable Worlds Observatory. You’ll learn about what instruments are planned and how those tools will help us locate habitable worlds and more. We discuss how UV light can erode atmospheres or fake biosignatures, why red dwarfs offer the most habitable real estate but are turbulent. Do planets need magnetic fields? Is there a way of detecting magnetic fields in far off solar systems? 

They also cover the roughly 6,000 known exoplanets, why most are still too faint and distant to study, and plans for a fleet of CubeSats to hunt for magnetic fields around habitable zone worlds. Finally, Neil reflects on the luxury of asking these questions, and how every answer widens the perimeter of our ignorance.

ABSTRACT
Most reorgs create confusion and friction. Spotify developed a more collaborative way of approaching org design, where teams help shape their missions, boundaries and structure.

This talk is a career experience report about taking the lessons from that work and applying a similar approach, which we now call Collaborative Org Design, years later at a fast-growing B2B scale-up facing a shift in strategy and team topology.

Joakim will share what worked, what didn’t, how his team used ideas from Team Topologies and self-selection, and how initial skepticism turned into comments like “this was the smoothest reorg I’ve ever seen.”

You’ll leave with practical patterns, pitfalls and facilitation tips for involving teams directly in org design.

items.title: How an Effort to Shield Coal Miners From Black Lung Fell Apart | FRONTLINE @NPR @pubhealthwatch
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Watch a video drawn from "Coal's Human Cost," a Nov. 2026 investigative documentary from @frontline, @NPR, @pubhealthwatch & the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom.  

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

When Johnathan Wright began working underground in coal mines more than 25 years ago, the percentage of veteran working coal miners in Central Appalachia diagnosed with black lung disease was down to roughly one in 10. 

Today, that reported rate is the highest it’s been since 1978: One in three — and Wright, age 44, has joined them.

“It’s awful,” says Wright, who was diagnosed with the incurable disease in 2023 after he started struggling to breathe when climbing the Kentucky hills, and began coughing up grey phlegm. “You work your whole life to enjoy the rest of it, and then you can't enjoy it.”

Wright is among the coal miners who share their stories in Coal’s Human Cost, a new documentary from FRONTLINE, NPR, Public Health Watch and the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom. Its Nov. 10, 2026, premiere comes as the Trump administration has been boosting coal mining, including through a pledge of nearly $700 million to keep coal-fired power plants running and coal exports flowing.

Against that backdrop, "Coal’s Human Cost" tracks the resurgence of black lung disease in Appalachia, the impact on miners and their families, and the role of the government and the mining industry in failing to protect them. 

“It just still amazes me after all these years that these conditions have not been improved," Ron Carson, a retired director of black lung clinics, tells correspondent Howard Berkes in the above video drawn from the documentary.

items.title: Archeologists Investigate The Space Dagger Inside King Tut's Tomb
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>A dagger fit for a king… forged from iron that fell from the sky. And that’s only the first surprise.

In this episode, cutting-edge scans and chemical tests reopen Egypt’s darkest and brightest mysteries. See how XRF proves Tutankhamun’s dagger is meteoric iron and why a scarab in his breastplate traces back to desert glass from the Great Sand Sea. Then travel beneath Saqqara, where CT scans expose millions of animal mummies—some complete, some parts, some startlingly empty—and why they still mattered. Inside newly found embalmers’ workshops, a long-sought secret emerges as natron in solution rewrites how bodies endured millennia. At Giza, laser mapping and a grid of ancient post holes reveal equinox-aligned precision behind the Great Pyramid’s near-perfect build. Finally, forensic clues from Armana’s child graves point to brutal labor, hunger, and a killer still with us today, while ingenious portcullises and hidden passages show how pharaohs fought tomb robbers.

Watch to uncover the science, the deception, and the devotion that shaped life, death, and eternity in ancient Egypt.

#Egypt #Tutankhamun #Pyramids #Mummies #Archaeology #Saqqara #AncientHistory</article>

items.title: Grokking the Brain: What AI Reveals About How You Learn • Barbara Oakley • GOTO Copenhagen 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This presentation was recorded at GOTO Copenhagen 2026. #GOTOcon #GOTOcph
Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Barbara Oakley - Professor of Engineering at Oakland University @BarbaraOakley 


RESOURCES
https://x.com/Barbara97881398
https://www.linkedin.com/in/barbaraoakley/
https://barbaraoakley.com/
https://gotopia.tech/experts/1554/barbara-oakley


ABSTRACT
Train an AI model long past the point where it has memorized its examples, and something strange happens — it stops memorizing and suddenly "groks" the pattern beneath them. That hard-won pattern can then be "distilled" into a smaller, faster model that runs it with ease. These are ideas from AI — but they may give us our clearest view yet of the human brain. We grok a hard skill slowly, with conscious effort, then distill it into a fast, automatic system that needs no effort at all. That is what expertise is.

The same “machinery” has a quieter side. A model is aligned by its training data — and in an analogous fashion, so are humans. Give me a child to the age of seven, the old saying goes, and I'll show you the adult. But adults are aligned too, usually without knowing it — and a brain aligned a little too well can harden into a mental fortress, deflecting new ideas.

Curiosity provides a way out. Dopamine—reward-based learning—fuels the brain's ability to rewire — it helps us build new links, keeps the fortress gate open, and keeps hard-won knowledge from setting into a wall. We'll look at what all this means for how you learn, how you use AI, and how you keep thinking for yourself in an age that makes it easy not to.

items.title: Archeologists Investigate Chester: Home To Britain's Largest Roman Amphitheatre
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>Chester hides a Roman story on a colossal scale. From a vanished gatehouse to an 8,000-seat arena, this town’s past still shapes its streets today.

We trace how the River Dee once brought Classis Britannica warships to a busy harbour beneath today’s racecourse, abseil the fortress walls to read Roman stonework up close, and step behind fencing to see the newly uncovered foundations of the North Gate. In the amphitheatre, baiting rings and rare finds reveal brutal spectacles — including evidence for a left-handed retiarius. Down in Alderley Edge, a hoard of Constantine-era coins and pick-marked tunnels expose Rome’s hunger for copper and the vivid blue pigment ceruleum. A lone shrine to Minerva still stands in its original spot, and a mysterious “elliptical building” hints at a bolder plan: Deva Victrix as a provincial capital under Agricola — with eyes on Ireland.

Discover why Chester may be Britain’s most Roman town, and what its stones still refuse to say. Watch now to see the full picture unfold.

#Chester #RomanBritain #DevaVictrix #Archaeology #HistoryDocumentary #BritainsMostHistoricTowns #Amphitheatre</article>

See bone skates that crossed frozen rivers, a fearsome shield wall in action, and combs that sparked a grooming craze. We handle a pristine 1,000-year-old coprolite to decode diet and parasites, examine a coin stamped with both St Peter and a Thor’s hammer, and get closer to Ulf’s extraordinary elephant-tusk horn inside York Minster. Then follow the trade routes that led to the Vale of York hoard and the shipbuilding innovation that powered them.

Discover how Vikings and Anglo-Saxons blended beliefs, businesses, and even street names to build a bustling, multicultural city. Watch to see why York’s Viking story still shapes the streets beneath your feet — and the clues hiding in plain sight.

Watch now to experience Viking York as you’ve never seen it.

items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/episodes/460

Artie Shevchenko - Software Engineer at Canva & Author of "Code Health Guardian" @artie_shevchenko 
Titus Winters - Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe & Co-Curator of "Software Engineering at Google" @tituscsucredu 

RESOURCES

Links
https://youtu.be/NNMnbBf0Itw
https://youtu.be/W7XL_LZgvKI
https://youtu.be/gAQ6t3F_2Ug

DESCRIPTION
Artie Shevchenko, a former Google engineer who is now at Canva and teaches at ITMO University, tells Titus Winters how his book “Code Health Guardian” came together: the internal code review classes he built at Google (over 1,000 Googlers attended, with a 4.5-star rating), a talk on A Philosophy of Software Design, and years of teaching a university course. He keeps that book's three complexity problems (change amplification, cognitive load, and unknown unknowns), which he says help you rank what to fix first. But he doesn't agree with its two causes, obscurity and dependencies. Dependencies are also the building blocks of all software, so he replaces them with six more specific causes: untrue interfaces, complex interfaces, unfamiliarity, too many dependencies, duplication, and unstable dependencies. Titus agrees that "all dependencies are bad" misses the point, since every dependency is both a benefit and a liability.

The AI conversation turns on understanding. Artie compares models to two types of exam students who give nearly identical answers: one who understands the material and one who memorized it. Most of the time you can get away with the second kind, but not always, so a human "code health guardian" still has to validate AI output or risk losing intellectual control of the codebase. He admits he's still learning how to prioritize reviews, and no longer reads every test line as carefully. Titus adds that his top worry is whatever is hardest to change later (dependencies, frameworks, state storage, API design, database schemas), which lines up with Artie's view that interfaces sit at the top of the list. They also discuss intellectual versus statistical control (tests as evidence), and Artie makes the case for "semi-functional programming," meaning immutability by default, which reduces obscurity. Titus ties it to testing: stateless code is trivial to test, and mutable state is where time enters the problem. Both stress that nobody has the full playbook for AI-assisted development yet.

Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Daniel Terhorst-North - Originator of Behavior Driven Development (BDD) & Principal at Dan North & Associates @daniel-terhorst-north 


RESOURCES

ABSTRACT
Oh great, another session about AI. Your social media feeds are already flooded with agentic this and spec-driven that; one-shot rewrites and everyone-is-a-programmer-now.

I am not using genAI to go faster but to go broader. It lets me offload (significant) side concerns in areas where I am competent but have no wish to become proficient; the time-sink supporting work that I would either hack together badly myself or side-step altogether.

I want to share some models and metaphors that are helping me make sense of this new world: why Ward Cunningham hates printers; how riding a fixie isn’t really cycling; why I'm treating Claude as a fantastic researcher and a terrible programmer; how test-first is the new TDD.

I am calling this adjacent engineering. Sometimes these side quests become significant enough to spin off into their own entire product, which I call adjacent discovery.

My goal is to give you a more nuanced take on generative AI, to help you cut through all the noise and get actual work done.

items.title: AI-Friendly Code: The Missing Link for Speed with Quality • Adam Tornhill • GOTO Copenhagen 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This presentation was recorded at GOTO Copenhagen 2026. #GOTOcon #GOTOcph
Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Adam Tornhill - Founder and CTO at CodeScene Programmer, psychologist, Lisp hacker, speaker and author of several books including "Your Code as a Crime Scene" @adamtornhill2546 


RESOURCES
https://x.com/AdamTornhill
https://www.linkedin.com/in/adam-tornhill-71759b48
https://www.adamtornhill.com/
https://github.com/adamtornhill
https://gotopia.tech/experts/3/adam-tornhill


ABSTRACT
Have you seen early productivity gains from AI, only to watch them disappear under growing complexity and production incidents? You're not alone. There's a common reason: many production systems already struggle with technical debt. When AI agents enter the development loop, that debt becomes a multiplier. Poor-quality code not only increases defects and costs. It dramatically raises AI risk by driving high breakage rates, turning promising AI agents into legacy code generators rather than genuine help.

Fortunately, there's hope on the horizon. In this talk, Adam Tornhill shows how organizations can achieve both speed and quality with AI. Backed by large-scale empirical studies on AI coding and developer productivity, we separate what works from what doesn't in real-world systems. Building on these findings, we then look at a practical framework for driving and sustaining AI-friendly code at scale. The AI revolution is here. Is your code ready?

items.title: THE MOST INFLUENTIAL ARTIST NOBODY KNOWS #history #arthistory #painting #artist #art
items.author: Great Art Explained
items.content:
<article>Pierre Puvis de Chavannes (1824–1898) was one of the most influential French painters of the nineteenth century, although today he is far less well known than many of the artists he inspired. At a time when Impressionism was transforming painting with its fascination for modern life, light and movement, Puvis looked in an entirely different direction. His paintings depict quiet, dreamlike worlds populated by mysterious figures in timeless landscapes, where very little seems to happen, yet everything feels strangely significant.

Best known for his monumental murals in public buildings, Puvis developed a distinctive style characterised by muted colours, simplified forms, flattened perspectives and an almost complete absence of drama. His figures often appear detached from reality, suspended somewhere between classical antiquity and the modern world.

Although his work might appear conservative today, it was remarkably innovative. By rejecting naturalism in favour of atmosphere, symbolism and emotional suggestion, Puvis helped open the door to modern art. His influence can be traced through Gauguin, Seurat, Matisse and even the young Picasso. He was admired by artists who would go on to challenge almost everything nineteenth-century painting stood for, making him one of the most important, and perhaps most overlooked, bridges between academic tradition and modernism.</article>

items.title: SCHUMANN: BIPOLAR OR BITONAL? #ghost #piano
items.author: Ben Laude
items.content:
<article>“The Ghost Variations,” Robert Schumann’s last work, are often heard as a musical representation of the auditory hallucinations he was experiencing at the time of its composition. The final variation is so dense with chromatic neighbor tones across a broken chorale texture that it’s possible to pronounce the entire theme in D major in the right hand amid a faint backdrop of E-flat major.

Credit to Peter Dugan and our mutual former teacher Matti Raekallio for drawing my attention to this chilling way of interpreting the final variation, and to @AshishXiangyiKumar for the idea of the variations “eavesdropping” on the theme.</article>

items.title: This Music is Haunted by Chopin
items.author: Ben Laude
items.content:
<article>Ben Laude performs George Crumb's "Dream Images (Love-Death Music)" from Makrokosmos, Volume I

American composer George Crumb (1929-2022) composed the first volume of "Makrokosmos" in 1972 for his friend David Burge. The work, subtitled "12 Fantasy-Pieces after the Zodiac for Amplified Piano," is known for its extended techniques and artfully notated score. Crumb identified his "spiritual impulse" in composing the music as akin to "the darker side of Chopin."

The eleventh piece, "Dream Images (Love-Death Music)," occupying the Gemini position in Crumb's zodiacal scheme, follows an eerie, recurring whisper of a half-remembered theme out of which the central subject of Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu fades in and out of the music's consciousness. (Crumb had originally intended to quote the 18th variation from Rachmaninoff’s ‘Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini,’ but replaced it with the Chopin passage in the final version due to copyright considerations.)

Crumb writes of his fascination with "the 'magical properties' of music" when composing Makrokosmos, among other "recurrent haunting images" such as "the problem of the origin of evil," "the 'timelessness' of time, "the haunting words of Pascal: 'The eternal silence of infinite space terrifies me'," and "these few lines of Rilke: 'And in the nights the heavy earth is falling from all the stars down into loneliness. We are falling. And yet there is One who holds this falling endlessly gently in his hands.'"

Performed on October 26, 2026 in Russell/Wanlass Performance Hall at Utah State University.

Production Director: Eddie Myers

items.title: The King Obsessed With Witches
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>Maddy Pelling and Anthony Delaney investigate one of Europe’s bloodiest witch hunts: Scotland’s North Berwick Witch trials of 1591. In this extraordinary case, fears escalated all the way up the social hierarchy to the King himself, James VI. A wild storm in the North Sea had nearly killed James and his new wife Anne of Denmark, fuelling his fascination with the intellectual study of demonology. A maelstrom of terror brought together the King’s paranoia of a conspiracy against him with local rivalries and misfortune, twisting together the fates of individuals from maidservants to magistrates, in the hunt for scapegoats.

Maddy and Anthony meet at Edinburgh’s Holyrood Palace, the place where the King himself interrogated one of the alleged witches, Agnes Sampson, a local healer and midwife. This was a remarkable moment when different worlds met, king and commoner, captured through the accounts of her confession.

But who were the accused, and how were their confessions extracted? Maddy and Anthony travel through this area of Scotland and examine the records to understand how the fear of witches spread through entire communities, and how the women and men of North Berwick were tragically caught up in the terror.

<article>What lies beyond the Event Horizon? 
Try Brilliant’s interactive tutor for free and get 20% off an annual Premium subscription at http://brilliant.org/astrum

▀▀▀▀▀▀

In all of space, nothing is more mind-meltingly strange than a black hole. These cosmic monsters are places where space becomes time, time becomes space, and the fundamental laws of physics simply cease to exist. But what if the event horizon isn't the final boundary?

Way past the point of no return, deep inside spinning Kerr black holes, lies a theoretical boundary even stranger than the first: the Cauchy Horizon. Beyond this threshold, spacetime breaks down entirely, cause and effect collapse, and physics yields to pure, unpredictable madness.

From the lethal trap of spaghettification to time-looping curves and infinite mass inflation, discover what happens when you attempt the ultimate one-way trip into the abyss....

items.title: What if you didn’t brush your teeth for a year? - Justin Merritt
items.author: TED-Ed
items.content:
<article>Trace the impact that not brushing or flossing can have on your teeth, gums, microbiome, and overall health over time.

--

At any given time, your mouth is maintaining a delicate balance between hundreds of microbial species, which is why dentists agree that you should brush twice and floss once every day. But what if you just… didn’t? If you stopped doing any oral hygiene, how long would it take for your mouth to get messy? Justin Merritt investigates how not brushing can impact your health over time.
